\paragraph{Drafter's summary.} logit P(churn) = -1.35 + a sparse linear backbone over 28 inputs (voicemail plan -1.05 per SD, international plan +0.80, voicemail messages +0.68, evening charge +0.40, state offsets) + a customer-service-calls threshold (an early hinge from 3 calls, off in state:29, plus a late chain from 5 calls gated by state:4/state:5: nothing for 0-2 calls, then about +2.3 logit per call from 4) + three day-usage hinges (nothing below about 200 day minutes, then rising in stages to +4.7 logit above 300 minutes; the first hinge starts about 54 minutes later with a voicemail plan) + exact single-state offsets, all additive in the logit. Day minutes and service calls have no linear term. Train AUC 0.888, accuracy 0.880. Compared with the run's cluster-1 lead (churn100-s4, key 24573), the same two thresholds (service calls, high day usage) carry the nonlinearity, but here day usage is gated by the voicemail plan rather than combined with evening minutes, there is no evening term beyond the linear charge, and many more single-state units.

\paragraph{What resisted explanation.} Nothing structural: no hidden node needed splitting (8 input splits, 1 consolidation of two customer-service-calls copies). 11 of the 21 hidden nodes are single-state offsets (exactly affine in one-hot indicators) and 5533 is never active on train (contributes exactly 0), so the nonlinearity sits in 8 nodes: the service-call hinges and the day-usage hinges. Near-cancelling state pairs: state:39 direct -2.85 vs unit +2.30 (net -0.55, empirical -0.93), state:46 -2.22 vs +0.77, state:33 +1.05 vs -0.68. The model is badly calibrated in level: mean prediction 0.082 against a base rate of 0.1415 (0-2 calls: 0.05-0.06 vs 0.11; 4 calls 0.21 vs 0.44), and over-confident from 6 calls (0.89-0.98 vs 0.55-0.68, 42 customers). state:18 gets +0.36 logit against an empirical -0.48 (65 rows); state:4 switches off the late service-call chain although its 41 customers churn more (empirical +0.80). closed\_\allowbreak{}form\_\allowbreak{}max\_\allowbreak{}abs\_\allowbreak{}err 0.028 (state\_\allowbreak{}offsets) is 3-significant-figure rounding; numeric error 1.8e-15.

\subsection{Plain-language summary}\label{app:churn100-s4-c3:plain}

Magnitudes are changes in predicted risk for a typical patient; confidence words follow the test-split check and n. The text describes what the model does, not the world.}}\par\smallskip
\paragraph{Summary (drafted).} For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, no international or voice-mail plan, no voice-mail messages, 1 call to customer service and median usage) the model predicts a chance of leaving of about 1\%; it adds up four parts: fixed-weight inputs, service calls, heavy daytime use and state units.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C054]}} This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights: an international plan raises a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 1\% to about 18\%, and a voice-mail plan lowers it to below 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C055, C063]}} More voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 1\% at 0 to about 6\% at 32 messages, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C056]}} A higher evening charge also raises it steadily, from about 1\% at 11.76 US dollars to about 2\% at 22.57 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C059]}} Through it, the state moves the chance from about 1\% in West Virginia to about 5\% in Washington and about 4\% in Nevada, and to below 1\% in Rhode Island, Hawaii and Vermont (72 to 82 training customers per state).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C057, C058, C061, C062, C064]}} This part adds up two parts: an early rise and a late rise in calls to customer service.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C090]}} From about 3 calls upwards it adds to the chance slowly at first, then faster: for a typical such customer, 4 calls take it from about 1\% to about 10\%, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C089]}} Up to 3 calls the chance rises slowly at first, then faster, from about 1\% to about 2\% for a typical customer, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C084]}} That early rise happens only outside Nebraska, California and Colorado: in Nebraska the chance stays at about 1\% from 0 to 3 calls, against a rise from about 1\% to about 2\% elsewhere, slowly at first, then faster, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C088]}} Daytime minutes add to the chance only once they rise above about 209 minutes, in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, from about 1\% at 0 minutes to about 16\% at 271 minutes, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C100]}} The rise is much larger without a voice-mail plan: from 112 to 249 daytime minutes the chance goes from about 1\% to about 6\% without one, but stays below 1\% with one, in an uneven way, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C099]}} This part acts on 1074 of 4000 training customers, 290 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 1\% without it and about 4\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C102]}} This part reads only the state: it raises a typical customer's chance from about 1\% to about 12\% in Rhode Island, to about 3\% in Vermont and to about 2\% in Tennessee.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C104, C105, C106]}} It lowers the chance to below 1\% in Virginia and in Nevada.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C107, C108]}}
\paragraph{The whole model.} The model adds up four parts into one score: fixed-weight inputs, service calls, heavy daytime use and state units.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C054]}} \textit{Evidence.} It is made up of these four parts (each explained below); the score is their sum, which was checked on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C054]}} Changing one input at a time across the whole model, an international plan takes a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 1\% to about 18\%, and a voice-mail plan lowers it to below 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C001, C008]}} More voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 1\% at 0 to about 6\% at 32 messages, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C002]}} More daytime minutes raise it in an uneven way, from about 1\% at 112 minutes to about 6\% at 249 minutes, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C003]}} The model ignores evening calls, evening minutes, international calls, the international charge, international minutes, night-time calls, the night-time charge and night-time minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C046, C047, C048, C049, C050, C051, C052, C053]}}
\paragraph{Fixed-weight inputs.} This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights: an international plan, voice-mail messages and the evening charge raise the chance of leaving, steadily for the numbers, and a voice-mail plan lowers it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C055, C056, C059, C063]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, an international plan takes a typical customer from about 1\% to about 18\%, and a voice-mail plan lowers the chance to below 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C055, C063]}} More voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 1\% at 0 to about 6\% at 32 messages, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C056]}} A higher evening charge also raises it steadily, from about 1\% at 11.76 US dollars to about 2\% at 22.57 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C059]}} Through it, the state moves the chance from about 1\% in West Virginia to about 5\% in Washington and about 4\% in Nevada, and to below 1\% in Rhode Island, Hawaii and Vermont (72 to 82 training customers per state).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C057, C058, C061, C062, C064]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C083]}}
\paragraph{Service calls.} This part raises the chance of leaving with calls to customer service, slowly at first, then faster from about 3 calls upwards; it adds up two parts.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C090, C089]}} \textit{Evidence.} It is made of two parts that are added: an early rise and a late rise in calls to customer service.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C090]}} From about 3 calls upwards it adds to the chance slowly at first, then faster: for a typical such customer, 4 calls take it from about 1\% to about 10\%, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C089]}} Up to 3 calls the chance rises slowly at first, then faster, from about 1\% to about 2\% for a typical customer, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C084]}} That early rise happens only outside Nebraska, California and Colorado: in Nebraska the chance stays at about 1\% from 0 to 3 calls, against a rise from about 1\% to about 2\% elsewhere, slowly at first, then faster, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C088]}}
\paragraph{Early rise in calls.} This part raises the chance of leaving from about 3 customer-service calls upwards, in an uneven way.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C094]}} \textit{Evidence.} It acts on 830 of 4000 training customers, 213 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 1\% without it and about 2\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C095]}} Through it, calls add to the chance only from about 3 calls upwards, in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, 4 calls take it from about 1\% to about 10\%, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C094]}} Up to 3 calls it raises the chance slowly at first, then faster, but only outside Nebraska: there from about 1\% to about 2\%, while in Nebraska it stays at about 1\%, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C093]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C096]}}
\paragraph{Late rise in calls.} This part raises the chance of leaving for a small group of customers, more in Colorado and less in California.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C122, C117, C118]}} \textit{Evidence.} It acts on 134 of 4000 training customers, 74 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 39\% without it and about 75\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C122]}} For the typical customer it acts on, the chance through it is about 75\% in Colorado and about 39\% in California, against about 52\% in other states.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C117, C118]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C123]}}
\paragraph{Heavy daytime use.} This part raises the chance of leaving for heavy daytime users: daytime minutes add to it only above about 209 minutes, in an uneven way, and much less with a voice-mail plan.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C100, C099]}} \textit{Evidence.} This part acts on 1074 of 4000 training customers, 290 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 1\% without it and about 4\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C102]}} Daytime minutes add to the chance only once they rise above about 209 minutes, in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, from about 1\% at 0 minutes to about 16\% at 271 minutes, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C100]}} The rise is much larger without a voice-mail plan: from 112 to 249 daytime minutes the chance goes from about 1\% to about 6\% without one, but stays below 1\% with one, in an uneven way, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C099]}} A voice-mail plan lowers it: for the typical customer it acts on, from about 4\% to about 2\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C098]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C103]}}
\paragraph{State units.} This part reads only the state: it raises the chance of leaving in Rhode Island, Vermont and Tennessee, and lowers it in Virginia and Nevada.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C104, C105, C106, C107, C108]}} \textit{Evidence.} This part reads only the state: it raises a typical customer's chance from about 1\% to about 12\% in Rhode Island, to about 3\% in Vermont and to about 2\% in Tennessee.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C104, C105, C106]}} It lowers the chance to below 1\% in Virginia and in Nevada.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C107, C108]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C116]}}
\paragraph{Worth checking against what is known.} Worth checking: for customers in Rhode Island the fixed-weight inputs lower the chance to below 1\% while the state units raise it to about 12\%, so overall it is about 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C061, C104, C025]}} Worth checking: for customers in Nevada the fixed-weight inputs raise the chance to about 4\% while the state units lower it to below 1\%, so overall it is about 2\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C058, C108, C018]}} Worth checking: the state moves the chance by several points (Washington about 5\%, Maine about 3\%, Hawaii below 1\%), based on 72 to 86 training customers per state.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C004, C006, C007]}} Worth checking: the model treats a voice-mail plan as lowering the chance of leaving but more voice-mail messages as raising it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C008, C002]}} Worth checking: the early rise with customer-service calls does not happen for customers in Nebraska.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C093]}}

\subsection{Coverage}\label{app:churn100-s4-c3:coverage}
Coverage is computed by the current code (the function behind the \texttt{get\_coverage} tool) under these conventions. \emph{Candidate nodes} are all nodes of the explained model state except the output nodes. A candidate node is \emph{covered} when some annotation of the hierarchy (a leaf, or a composition together with its descendants) contains it and all its enabled outgoing edges. \emph{Exact Null} parts, which have no effect on any output for any input, count as covered: nodes with no path to an output over enabled, non-zero-weight edges (disconnected inputs and dead ends), and edges that have zero weight or touch such a node. Compositional coverage is the fraction of required compositions present: every annotation except a single global root containing every output must have a parent; a parentless, childless annotation made only of Null nodes is exempt.

\textbf{Hypothesis.} Root: logit P(churn) = -1.35 + linear\_\allowbreak{}backbone (identity\_\allowbreak{}lin) + service\_\allowbreak{}calls (identity\_\allowbreak{}svc) + 1.48*3118 + 1.50*4000 + 1.89*10131 (day\_\allowbreak{}usage\_\allowbreak{}hinges) + the state\_\allowbreak{}offsets units (-1.11*1295 - 1.25*7872 - 1.17*1390 - 0.56*5786 + small terms; 5533 is never active), purely additive in the logit; the sigmoid is the only coupling. 30 inputs are unconnected (international minutes, calls and charge, night minutes/\allowbreak{}charge/\allowbreak{}calls,\allowbreak{} evening minutes and calls, area codes 408/510 and 20 state indicators) and have zero effect. Train AUC 0.8884, accuracy 0.8795; the mean predicted churn is 0.082 against a base rate of 0.1415 (the model ranks well but under-predicts). Performance sources (train): all children replaced by least-squares linear fits gives AUC 0.8352 (an L2 logistic regression refit on all 71 inputs gets 0.8433); restoring day\_\allowbreak{}usage\_\allowbreak{}hinges alone gives 0.8713, service\_\allowbreak{}calls alone 0.8657, both 0.8884; the state units restore nothing (exactly linear). So the gain over linear (+0.053) comes from the day-usage and service-call thresholds, which are complementary.
